decks.title: Entropy, Free Energy and Spontaneity — Part 1: Spontaneous change, the second law and entropy
goals: Explain why the first law and the sign of ΔH cannot decide whether a change occurs, and state the second law
Describe entropy as a state function and a measure of disorder; predict the sign of ΔS and calculate ΔS = q_rev / T
Use the entropy change of the universe as the criterion of spontaneity and describe the thermal death of the universe

slides.heading: Why do some changes happen and others do not?
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **direction of change**. The first law counts energy; the **second law** and **entropy** tell us which way a change goes.

nodes.label: Entropy S and ΔS = q_rev / T

visual.alt: Flow chart of the topics of Part 1

slides.narration: Welcome to Part One. The first law of thermodynamics says that energy is conserved, but it cannot tell us which changes will actually happen. In this part we meet spontaneous processes, the second law, and entropy, a measure of disorder, and we learn to calculate entropy changes.

slides.heading: The first law is not enough
slides.body_md: The **first law** says energy is conserved. It does **not** say in which direction a change goes. Heat flowing from a cold body to a hot body would conserve energy, but never happens unaided. A negative **ΔH** is not a reliable guide either: **ice melts** above 273 K and **NH₄NO₃ dissolves** although both absorb heat.

rows: Heat from hot to cold body
Heat from cold to hot body (no work)

visual.alt: Table showing that neither energy conservation nor the sign of ΔH decides whether a change occurs

slides.narration: The first law only says that energy is conserved. Heat flowing from a cold body to a hot body would obey it, yet it does not happen by itself. Nor is the sign of the enthalpy change a reliable guide, because ice melts and ammonium nitrate dissolves, although both take in heat.

slides.heading: Two spontaneous changes
slides.body_md: A **spontaneous process** occurs of its own accord under the given conditions, in a definite direction. A gas **expands** into a vacuum; heat flows from **hot to cold**. The reverse changes need **outside work**: they are **non-spontaneous**.

visual.caption: Energy is conserved in the reverse changes too, but they do not occur unaided.

slides.narration: Here are two spontaneous changes. When the tap is opened, gas spreads into the empty bulb and never collects in one bulb again by itself. Heat flows from the hot body to the cold body, and never in the opposite direction unless work is done. Spontaneous changes have a definite direction.

slides.heading: Spontaneous and non-spontaneous; the second law
slides.body_md: **Spontaneous:** occurs unaided (rusting, dissolving, cooling). **Non-spontaneous:** needs outside work (pumping water uphill, compressing a gas). **Second law (Clausius):** heat cannot flow of itself from a colder to a hotter body. **(Kelvin–Planck):** heat from a single reservoir cannot be converted completely into work in a cycle. Both lead to: **the entropy of the universe increases in a spontaneous change**.

rows: Heat flows from hot to cold
Heat flows from cold to hot
Gas compresses itself into a corner

visual.alt: Table of spontaneous changes and their non-spontaneous reverses

slides.narration: A spontaneous process happens unaided, like rusting or the cooling of hot tea. A non spontaneous process needs outside work, like pumping water uphill. The second law has two familiar statements: heat does not flow by itself from cold to hot, and heat from a single source cannot be changed completely into work in a cycle.

slides.heading: Quick check: which change is non-spontaneous?
slides.body_md: Ask which direction of change you have ever seen happen on its own.
slides.narration: Quick check. For each change, think about whether you have ever seen it happen on its own at room temperature. Changes such as rusting, dissolving and cooling are natural. Look for the one that would need work to be done on the system before it could occur.

slides.heading: Entropy: disorder and a state function
slides.body_md: **Entropy, S,** measures the **disorder** (randomness) of a system. It is a **state function**: ΔS depends only on the initial and final states. For a **reversible** change **ΔS = q_rev / T**, in **J K⁻¹**. Entropy **rises** when a solid melts, a liquid boils, a gas is formed, a solute dissolves, or the volume of a gas increases; it **falls** when gas molecules combine.

visual.alt: Table of the sign of the entropy change for common processes

slides.narration: Entropy measures the disorder of a system, and it is a state function, so its change depends only on the initial and final states. For a reversible change, the entropy change is the heat divided by the temperature. Melting, boiling, dissolving and making a gas increase entropy, while molecules combining decrease it.

slides.heading: Entropy of water rises with temperature
slides.body_md: The entropy of a perfect crystal is **zero at 0 K** and **rises** as the temperature rises, with **jumps** at the melting point (**+22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**) and the boiling point (**+109.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**). Gas ≫ liquid > solid.

slides.narration: This graph shows the entropy of one mole of water. It starts at zero at absolute zero, rises as ice warms, and jumps when the ice melts. It rises again in the liquid and jumps much more when the water boils. Steam has the highest entropy because its molecules move freely.

slides.heading: Entropy of fusion and vaporisation: ΔS = ΔH / T
slides.body_md: At the melting or boiling point the change is **reversible** and takes in heat q = ΔH at constant T, so **ΔS = ΔH / T** (convert kJ to J). Vaporisation gives a much larger ΔS than fusion because a gas is much more disordered than a liquid.

visual.alt: Table of entropies of fusion and vaporisation

slides.narration: At the melting point or boiling point the change is reversible, and the heat absorbed equals the enthalpy change. So the entropy change is the enthalpy change divided by the temperature. Remember to convert kilojoules to joules. Vaporisation gives a much larger entropy change than fusion, because a gas is far more disordered than a liquid.

slides.heading: Worked example: entropy of vaporisation of benzene
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Benzene boils at 353.2 K with $\Delta_{vap}H = 30.8$ kJ mol⁻¹. Find $\Delta_{vap}S$.

$\Delta S = \dfrac{q_{rev}}{T} = \dfrac{30800\ \text{J mol}^{-1}}{353.2\ \text{K}} = 87.2$ J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the calculation of the entropy of vaporisation of benzene

slides.narration: Change the enthalpy of vaporisation into joules, which gives thirty thousand eight hundred joules for each mole. Divide by the boiling temperature, three hundred fifty three point two kelvin. The entropy of vaporisation of benzene is about eighty seven joules per kelvin per mole, close to the value for many liquids.

slides.heading: Quick check: entropy of vaporisation
slides.body_md: Convert kJ to J before dividing by the boiling point in kelvin.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the enthalpy of vaporisation in joules per mole, since the unit of entropy involves joules. Divide by the boiling point in kelvin. The result should be close to the values you saw in the table for other liquids, around ninety joules per kelvin per mole.

slides.heading: Entropy change on isothermal expansion of an ideal gas
slides.body_md: For a **reversible isothermal** expansion, $\Delta U = 0$, so $q_{rev} = -w = nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$ and **$\Delta S = nR\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$**. ΔS is positive on expansion (more room for the molecules) and negative on compression. It depends on the volume ratio only, not on T.

visual.alt: Table of entropy changes for the isothermal expansion and compression of an ideal gas

slides.narration: In a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas the internal energy does not change, so the heat absorbed equals the work done, n R T times the natural logarithm of the volume ratio. Dividing by the temperature, the entropy change is n R times the logarithm of the volume ratio. It is positive for expansion and negative for compression.

slides.heading: Worked example: expansion of 2 mol of gas
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two moles of an ideal gas expand reversibly and isothermally at 300 K from 10 L to 40 L. Find ΔS ($R = 8.314$ J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

$\Delta S = nR\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = 2 \times 8.314 \times \ln 4 = 2 \times 8.314 \times 1.386 \approx 23.05$ J K⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the entropy change for an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas

slides.narration: The volume ratio is four, and the natural logarithm of four is one point three eight six. Multiply by the number of moles and the gas constant. The entropy of the gas rises by about twenty three joules per kelvin. The heat absorbed reversibly at three hundred kelvin is the temperature times this, about seven kilojoules.

slides.heading: Quick check: halving the pressure
slides.body_md: Doubling the volume gives ln 2 = 0.693 in the formula.
slides.narration: Quick check. The gas expands until its volume is doubled, so the volume ratio is two. Use the formula with the number of moles, the gas constant and the natural logarithm of two. The temperature itself does not appear in the final formula for the entropy change.

slides.heading: Entropy of the universe decides
slides.body_md: **ΔS(universe) = ΔS(system) + ΔS(surroundings)**, with **ΔS(surroundings) = −ΔH / T**. A change is spontaneous if **ΔS(universe) > 0**. Melting of 1 mol of ice: at 283 K the total is **+0.8 J K⁻¹** (melts); at 263 K it is **−0.8 J K⁻¹** (does not melt).

visual.caption: ΔS(universe) > 0 for a spontaneous change.

slides.narration: Here the system is one mole of ice. Its entropy rises by twenty two joules per kelvin when it melts. The surroundings lose the same heat, so their entropy falls by the heat divided by their temperature. At two hundred eighty three kelvin the total is positive, so ice melts. At two hundred sixty three kelvin the total is negative, so it does not.

slides.heading: Second law in terms of entropy; thermal death
slides.body_md: **Second law:** in a spontaneous (irreversible) process the **entropy of the universe increases**; in a reversible process it is unchanged; it **never decreases**. As changes continue, the entropy of the universe heads to a **maximum**: **thermal death**, a state of uniform temperature in which no heat flows and no work can be got from heat.

nodes.label: Uniform temperature: no work from heat

visual.alt: Flow chart from spontaneous change to the thermal death of the universe

slides.narration: The second law says that the entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous change, stays constant in a reversible one, and never decreases. If this goes on, the entropy of the universe tends towards a maximum. That is the so called thermal death, with the same temperature everywhere, no flow of heat, and no work to be had from heat.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: The first law does not give the direction of change; ΔH < 0 is neither necessary nor sufficient for spontaneity.
A spontaneous process occurs unaided in one direction; the reverse is non-spontaneous and needs work.
Entropy S: disorder, a state function; ΔS = q_rev / T (J K⁻¹); ΔS(fusion or vaporisation) = ΔH / T.
Isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas: ΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁).
Spontaneous if ΔS(universe) = ΔS(system) − ΔH/T > 0; the universe tends to thermal death.

visual.alt: Summary table of the key ideas of Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part One. The first law does not give the direction of change. Spontaneous processes happen unaided, and the second law says that the entropy of the universe increases in them. Entropy is a state function, measuring disorder, and at a phase change it is the enthalpy change divided by the temperature.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Convert ΔH from kJ to J before dividing by T to get ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Use the reversible heat: ΔS = q_rev / T, not the actual heat of an irreversible change.
Predict the sign of ΔS by looking at the change in the number of moles of gas and at changes of state.
For the universe add ΔS(system) and ΔS(surroundings) = −ΔH / T for the same temperature.
Say "entropy of the universe increases" in a spontaneous change, not "entropy of the system".

decks.title: Entropy, Free Energy and Spontaneity — Part 2: Gibbs and Helmholtz energy, ΔG° and K, the third law
goals: Define the Gibbs and Helmholtz free energies, relate them, and use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS to judge spontaneity and find a crossover temperature
Calculate K from ΔG° and ΔG° from K using ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K
State the third law of thermodynamics and use standard entropies

slides.heading: A single criterion: free energy
slides.body_md: Part 2: combining ΔH and ΔS into **free energy**, the criterion of spontaneity, its link with the **equilibrium constant**, and the **third law**.

visual.alt: Table of the free-energy functions

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. Looking at the system and the surroundings together is awkward, so we combine them into a single function of the system, the free energy. We meet the Gibbs and Helmholtz free energies, use them to decide spontaneity and the crossover temperature, link them to the equilibrium constant, and state the third law.

slides.heading: Gibbs and Helmholtz free energy
slides.body_md: **Gibbs energy G = H − TS**; at constant T and p, **ΔG = ΔH − TΔS**. **Helmholtz energy A = U − TS**; at constant T, ΔA = ΔU − TΔS. Both are **state functions**. −ΔG is the **maximum useful (non-expansion) work**; −ΔA is the maximum work of all kinds at constant temperature.

visual.alt: Table comparing Gibbs and Helmholtz energies

slides.narration: The Gibbs energy is the enthalpy minus the temperature times the entropy, and it is the one used at constant temperature and pressure. The Helmholtz energy is the internal energy minus the temperature times the entropy, used at constant temperature and volume. Both are state functions, and a negative change means a spontaneous process.

slides.heading: The relation G = A + pV
slides.body_md: Since $H = U + pV$: $G = H - TS = U + pV - TS = (U - TS) + pV$, so **G = A + pV**. At constant T: $\Delta G = \Delta A + \Delta(pV)$. For ideal gases $\Delta(pV) = \Delta n_g RT$, so **ΔG = ΔA + Δn_g RT**. For reactions without a change in the number of moles of gas, ΔG ≈ ΔA.

visual.alt: Table of the difference between ΔG and ΔA for gaseous reactions at 300 K

slides.narration: Start from the definition of the Gibbs energy. Replace the enthalpy by internal energy plus pressure times volume. Grouping the internal energy minus T S gives the Helmholtz energy, so G equals A plus p V. For ideal gases the change in p V is the change in moles of gas times R T, which is zero if the moles of gas do not change.

slides.heading: Criteria for spontaneity: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
slides.body_md: At constant T and p: **ΔG < 0** spontaneous; **ΔG = 0** equilibrium; **ΔG > 0** non-spontaneous (the reverse occurs). The signs of ΔH and ΔS decide how the answer depends on **temperature**. At the crossover, **T = ΔH / ΔS**.

visual.alt: Table of the four sign combinations of ΔH and ΔS and the spontaneity of the reaction

slides.narration: At constant temperature and pressure, a negative change in Gibbs energy means spontaneous, zero means equilibrium, and positive means non spontaneous. The signs of the enthalpy and entropy changes decide how this depends on temperature. When both have the same sign there is a crossover temperature, equal to the enthalpy change divided by the entropy change.

slides.heading: ΔG against temperature
slides.body_md: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is a **straight line** in T with slope −ΔS. **N₂O₄ → 2NO₂** (ΔH, ΔS > 0): the line falls and crosses zero at **325 K**; spontaneous above. **2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂** (ΔH, ΔS < 0): the line rises, crossing zero at **780 K**; spontaneous below.

slides.narration: The Gibbs energy change is a straight line against temperature, with slope equal to minus the entropy change. For the dissociation of dinitrogen tetroxide, both changes are positive, so the line falls and crosses zero at about three hundred twenty five kelvin. For nitric oxide and oxygen, both are negative, so the line rises and crosses zero near seven hundred eighty kelvin.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔH° and ΔS° of the Haber reaction
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)}$ find ΔH° and ΔS° from ΔfH°(NH₃) = −46.1 kJ mol⁻¹ and S° (N₂ 191.6, H₂ 130.7, NH₃ 192.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

$\Delta H^\circ = 2(-46.1) = -92.2$ kJ. $\Delta S^\circ = 2(192.5) - [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = 385.0 - 583.7 = -198.7$ J K⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the calculation of the enthalpy and entropy changes for ammonia synthesis

slides.narration: The enthalpy change is twice the formation enthalpy of ammonia, since the elements contribute zero. For entropy, add the standard entropies of the products and subtract those of the reactants. Four moles of gas become two, so the entropy change is negative, about minus one hundred ninety nine joules per kelvin.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Helmholtz criterion
slides.body_md: Compare with ΔG < 0 at constant T and p: which variables are held constant for A?
slides.narration: Quick check. The Helmholtz energy is the internal energy minus T S, and it is the natural function when the temperature and the volume are held constant. Recall the sign of the change in the Gibbs energy for a spontaneous process, and use the same sign for the Helmholtz energy.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔG° at 298 K and the crossover temperature
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Using $\Delta H^\circ = -92.2$ kJ and $\Delta S^\circ = -198.7$ J K⁻¹ for ammonia synthesis, find ΔG° at 298 K and the temperature at which it becomes zero.

$\Delta G^\circ = -92.2 - 298 \times (-0.1987) = -92.2 + 59.2 = -33.0$ kJ. $T = \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S} = \dfrac{92\,200}{198.7} = 464$ K.

visual.alt: Table of the Gibbs energy change at 298 K and the crossover temperature for ammonia synthesis

slides.narration: Convert the entropy change to kilojoules per kelvin. The temperature times minus the entropy change is plus fifty nine kilojoules. Adding the enthalpy change gives a Gibbs energy change of about minus thirty three kilojoules, so the reaction is spontaneous at room temperature. Setting it to zero gives a crossover near four hundred sixty four kelvin, above which it is not spontaneous.

slides.heading: Quick check: converting ΔS to kilojoules
slides.body_md: ΔH is in kJ and ΔS is in J K⁻¹: use the same energy unit.
slides.narration: Quick check. The enthalpy change is given in kilojoules but the entropy change is in joules per kelvin. Express both in the same unit before you subtract. Remember also that the temperature must be in kelvin, and that a negative entropy change makes the temperature term positive.

slides.heading: ΔG° and the equilibrium constant

slides.narration: At equilibrium the Gibbs energy change is zero, and the standard Gibbs energy change is related to the equilibrium constant. It equals minus two point three oh three R T times the logarithm of K. A negative value gives K greater than one, a positive value gives K less than one, and zero gives K equal to one.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔG° from K
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A reaction has $K = 2.0 \times 10^{3}$ at 300 K. Find ΔG°.

$\Delta G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K = -2.303 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times \log(2.0 \times 10^3) = -5744 \times 3.30 \approx -19.0$ kJ mol⁻¹ (after dividing by 1000).

visual.alt: Table of the calculation of the standard Gibbs energy change from an equilibrium constant

slides.narration: Work out two point three oh three R T at three hundred kelvin, which is about five thousand seven hundred forty four joules per mole. The logarithm of two thousand is three point three. Multiply and change the sign, giving about minus nineteen kilojoules per mole. The sign is negative, as expected for a constant greater than one.

slides.heading: Quick check: from ΔG° to log K
slides.body_md: Rearrange ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K for log K, using joules.
slides.narration: Quick check. Rearrange the relation so that the logarithm of K is on one side. The standard Gibbs energy change is given in kilojoules, so convert it to joules to match the gas constant. Divide by two point three oh three R T and keep the sign carefully.

slides.heading: The third law and absolute entropy
slides.body_md: **Third law:** the entropy of a **perfect crystalline substance is zero at the absolute zero** of temperature. It gives entropy a natural zero, so **absolute (standard molar) entropies S°** can be tabulated. S° is **small** for compact solids and **large** for gases.

visual.alt: Table of standard molar entropies of some substances

slides.narration: The third law states that the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at the absolute zero of temperature. This gives entropy a natural zero, so absolute entropies can be listed in tables. Compact solids such as diamond have very small values, liquids have more, and gases have the largest values.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔS° from standard entropies
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find ΔS° and the crossover temperature for $\ce{2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ with S° (NO 210.8, O₂ 205.1, NO₂ 240.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) and ΔH° = -114.2 kJ.

$\Delta S^\circ = 2(240.1) - [2(210.8) + 205.1] = 480.2 - 626.7 = -146.5$ J K⁻¹. $T = \dfrac{114\,200}{146.5} = 780$ K: spontaneous below this.

visual.alt: Table of the calculation of the entropy change and crossover temperature for the oxidation of nitric oxide

slides.narration: Add the standard entropies of the products, two moles of nitrogen dioxide, and subtract those of the reactants. Three moles of gas become two, so the entropy change is negative, about minus one hundred forty six point five. The enthalpy change is also negative, so the reaction is spontaneous only below the crossover, near seven hundred eighty kelvin.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: G = H − TS; A = U − TS; G = A + pV, so ΔG = ΔA + Δn_g RT for ideal gases.
Constant T, p: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; ΔG < 0 spontaneous, = 0 equilibrium, > 0 non-spontaneous.
(−, +) always spontaneous; (+, −) never; (−, −) below ΔH/ΔS; (+, +) above ΔH/ΔS.
ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K: negative ΔG° gives K > 1; 2.303 RT = 5.706 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K.
Third law: S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K; ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants).

visual.alt: Summary table of the key ideas of Part 2

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part Two. The Gibbs energy is enthalpy minus T S, and the Helmholtz energy is internal energy minus T S. A negative Gibbs energy change means spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure. The signs of the enthalpy and entropy changes give the crossover temperature. The standard change links to the equilibrium constant, and the third law fixes absolute entropies.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Write ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with ΔH in kJ and TΔS in kJ (divide ΔS in J by 1000); T in kelvin.
For the crossover temperature use T = ΔH / ΔS with both in joules (or both in kilojoules).
In ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K use R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and ΔG° in joules.
State the conditions: ΔG < 0 at constant T and p; ΔA < 0 at constant T and V.
Define S = 0 only for a perfect crystal at 0 K when stating the third law.

In the equation linking the standard Gibbs energy change to K, use joules and check the sign. And when you state the third law, say a perfect crystalline substance at the absolute zero.

notes.title: Entropy, Free Energy and Spontaneity — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Inadequacy of the first law; spontaneous processes; the second law
sections.body_md:
The **first law** states that energy is conserved but gives **no direction** of change: heat flowing from a cold to a hot body would conserve energy. A negative ΔH is also not a sufficient criterion: ice melts above 273 K and NH₄NO₃ dissolves in water although both absorb heat.

A **spontaneous process** occurs of its own accord under the given conditions, in a definite direction (heat from hot to cold, gas into a vacuum, rusting). A **non-spontaneous process** needs outside work. A **reversible** process proceeds by infinitesimal steps with the system always in equilibrium.

**Second law:** (Clausius) heat cannot flow of itself from a colder to a hotter body; (Kelvin–Planck) heat from a single reservoir cannot be converted completely into work in a cycle. In terms of entropy: the **entropy of the universe increases** in a spontaneous change.

key_terms.definition_md: A process that occurs of its own accord, without continuous outside help, under the given conditions.
A process carried out in infinitesimal steps, the system being in equilibrium with its surroundings at every stage.
The entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous process.

sections.heading: 2. Entropy and its meaning
sections.body_md:
**Entropy S** is a measure of the **disorder** (randomness) of a system, and a **state function**. For a **reversible** change $\Delta S = q_{rev}/T$ (unit J K⁻¹; molar entropy J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

ΔS is **positive** for melting, vaporisation, sublimation, dissolution of a solid, formation of gas molecules and expansion of a gas; **negative** for freezing, condensation and the combination of gas molecules (2NO₂ → N₂O₄). S increases with temperature, with jumps at the melting and boiling points; S(gas) ≫ S(liquid) > S(solid).

key_terms.definition_md: A state function that measures the disorder of a system; ΔS = q_rev / T.
A property whose change depends only on the initial and final states.

sections.heading: 3. Calculating ΔS; entropy of the universe; thermal death
sections.body_md:
**At a phase change** (reversible, constant T): $\Delta S = \Delta H/T$ (ΔH in J). Ice 22.0 (fusion), water 109.1 (vaporisation), benzene 87.2 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (vaporisation). **Isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas:** $\Delta S = nR\ln(V_2/V_1)$.

**Entropy of the universe:** $\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr}$, with $\Delta S_{surr} = -\Delta H/T$. Spontaneous if ΔS(univ) > 0; zero at equilibrium. Ice melting at 283 K: +22.0 − 21.2 = +0.8 J K⁻¹ (melts); at 263 K: −0.8 J K⁻¹ (does not).

**Thermal death:** since the entropy of the universe keeps increasing, it tends to a maximum: uniform temperature, no heat flow, no work obtainable from heat.

key_terms.definition_md: The sum of the entropy changes of the system and the surroundings.
The predicted final state of the universe, with maximum entropy and uniform temperature, in which no work can be got from heat.

sections.heading: 4. Gibbs and Helmholtz free energy
sections.body_md:
**Gibbs energy** $G = H - TS$; at constant T and p, $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, and $-\Delta G = T\Delta S_{univ}$. **Helmholtz energy** $A = U - TS$; at constant T and V, ΔA < 0 is the criterion. −ΔG is the maximum useful (non-expansion) work; −ΔA is the maximum work of all kinds.

**Relationship:** $G = H - TS = U + pV - TS = A + pV$, so $\Delta G = \Delta A + \Delta(pV)$; for ideal gases $\Delta G = \Delta A + \Delta n_g RT$ (about 2.49 kJ per unit Δn_g at 300 K).

key_terms.definition_md: G = H − TS; the criterion of spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure is ΔG < 0.
A = U − TS; the criterion of spontaneity at constant temperature and volume is ΔA < 0.

sections.heading: 5. Criteria of spontaneity and the crossover temperature
sections.body_md:
$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. **(−, +):** always spontaneous. **(+, −):** never. **(−, −):** spontaneous at low T, below $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$. **(+, +):** spontaneous at high T, above $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$ (use consistent units).

Examples: N₂O₄ → 2NO₂ (ΔH = +57.2 kJ, ΔS = +175.9 J K⁻¹): ΔG° at 298 K = +4.78 kJ, spontaneous above 325 K. 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ (ΔH = −114.2, ΔS = −146.5): spontaneous below 780 K. MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂ (+100.7 kJ, +175.0 J K⁻¹): above 575 K.

key_terms.definition_md: The temperature T = ΔH / ΔS at which ΔG = 0 and the direction of spontaneity changes.

sections.heading: 6. ΔG° and the equilibrium constant; the third law
sections.body_md:
At equilibrium ΔG = 0 and $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303RT\log K$. ΔG° < 0: K > 1; ΔG° > 0: K < 1; ΔG° = 0: K = 1. At 298 K, 2.303 RT = 5.706 kJ mol⁻¹: ΔG° = −28.5 kJ gives log K = 4.99; ethanoic acid, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, has ΔG° = +27.1 kJ mol⁻¹.

**Third law:** the entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is **zero at the absolute zero**. It allows **absolute entropies** to be tabulated (S°: diamond 2.4, H₂O(l) 69.9, H₂O(g) 188.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), and $\Delta S^\circ = \sum S^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum S^\circ(\text{reactants})$.

The entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is zero at the absolute zero of temperature.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Dividing ΔH in kJ by T and quoting J K⁻¹ (convert to J first), or mixing kJ and J in ΔH − TΔS.
- Using the actual heat of an irreversible change in q/T instead of the reversible heat.
- Saying the entropy of the system must increase in a spontaneous change (it is the universe).
- Using T in °C, or ΔG° in kJ with R in J, in ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K.
- Forgetting to mention constant T and p for ΔG, and constant T and V for ΔA.
- Stating the third law without "perfect crystalline" and "absolute zero".

**How marks are usually awarded**
- ΔS at a phase change: convert ΔH to J (1), divide by T (1), unit (1).
- ΔG = ΔH − TΔS: consistent units (1), value with sign (1), conclusion about spontaneity (1).
- Crossover temperature: ΔG = 0 (1), T = ΔH / ΔS (1), direction above or below (1).
- ΔG° and K: 2.303 RT in joules (1), log K with sign (1), K (1).

cards.front_md: Why is the first law inadequate for predicting the direction of change?
cards.back_md: It only conserves energy; heat flow from cold to hot would also conserve it, and ΔH < 0 is neither necessary nor sufficient.

cards.front_md: Define a spontaneous process.
cards.back_md: A process that occurs of its own accord under the given conditions, in a definite direction, without continuous outside help.

cards.front_md: Give two examples of spontaneous and two of non-spontaneous processes.
cards.back_md: Spontaneous: heat from hot to cold, gas into a vacuum. Non-spontaneous: gas compressing itself, water flowing uphill.

cards.front_md: Give two endothermic spontaneous changes.
cards.back_md: Melting of ice above 273 K; dissolving of ammonium nitrate in water.

cards.front_md: State the Clausius form of the second law.
cards.back_md: Heat cannot flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter body.

cards.front_md: State the second law in terms of entropy.
cards.back_md: The entropy of the universe increases in a spontaneous process.

cards.front_md: What is a reversible process?
cards.back_md: One carried out in infinitesimal steps with the system in equilibrium with its surroundings at every stage.

cards.front_md: What is entropy?
cards.back_md: A state function that measures the disorder of a system; ΔS = q_rev / T.

cards.front_md: Why is entropy a state function?
cards.back_md: Its change depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path.

cards.front_md: Unit of entropy and of molar entropy?
cards.back_md: J K⁻¹ and J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Sign of ΔS for melting, boiling, dissolving a salt?
cards.back_md: Positive in all three (more disorder).

cards.front_md: Sign of ΔS for 2NO₂(g) → N₂O₄(g)?
cards.back_md: Negative: fewer moles of gas.

cards.front_md: ΔS at a melting or boiling point?
cards.back_md: $\Delta S = \Delta H / T$, with ΔH in J mol⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Entropies of fusion of ice and vaporisation of water?
cards.back_md: 22.0 and 109.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

cards.front_md: ΔS for the isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas?
cards.back_md: $\Delta S = nR\ln(V_2/V_1)$.

cards.front_md: ΔS of the surroundings for a process with enthalpy change ΔH at T?
cards.back_md: $\Delta S_{surr} = -\Delta H / T$.

cards.front_md: Criterion of spontaneity using the entropy of the universe?
cards.back_md: ΔS(universe) = ΔS(system) + ΔS(surroundings) > 0.

cards.front_md: What is the thermal death of the universe?
cards.back_md: The predicted final state of maximum entropy and uniform temperature, with no heat flow and no work obtainable from heat.

cards.front_md: Define the Gibbs free energy.
cards.back_md: G = H − TS; at constant T and p a process is spontaneous if ΔG < 0.

cards.front_md: Define the Helmholtz free energy.
cards.back_md: A = U − TS; at constant T and V a process is spontaneous if ΔA < 0.

cards.front_md: Relationship between G and A?
cards.back_md: G = A + pV, so ΔG = ΔA + Δn_g RT for ideal gases.

cards.front_md: What does −ΔG represent?
cards.back_md: The maximum useful (non-expansion) work obtainable at constant T and p.

cards.front_md: The Gibbs equation?
cards.back_md: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$.

cards.front_md: ΔH negative, ΔS positive: when spontaneous?
cards.back_md: At all temperatures.

cards.front_md: ΔH positive, ΔS negative: when spontaneous?
cards.back_md: At no temperature.

cards.front_md: ΔH and ΔS both positive: when spontaneous?
cards.back_md: At high temperature, above T = ΔH / ΔS.

cards.front_md: ΔH and ΔS both negative: when spontaneous?
cards.back_md: At low temperature, below T = ΔH / ΔS.

cards.front_md: Crossover temperature of N₂O₄ → 2NO₂ (+57.2 kJ, +175.9 J K⁻¹)?
cards.back_md: T = 57 200 / 175.9 = 325 K; spontaneous above.

cards.front_md: Relation between ΔG° and K?
cards.back_md: $\Delta G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$.

cards.front_md: What does a negative ΔG° imply about K?
cards.back_md: K > 1: products favoured at equilibrium.

cards.front_md: Value of 2.303 RT at 298 K?
cards.back_md: 5.706 kJ mol⁻¹ (5706 J mol⁻¹).

cards.front_md: State the third law of thermodynamics.
cards.back_md: The entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is zero at the absolute zero of temperature.

questions.stem_md: A physics teacher lists four changes that all conserve energy. Which one cannot happen as a spontaneous change, even though it does not break the first law?

options.text_md: heat passing from the hot block to the cold block
heat passing from a cold block to a hot block in contact with it, with no work done
a gas spreading into a neighbouring evacuated vessel
the pressure of a gas cylinder falling when its valve is opened

questions.solution_md: The first law only says that energy is conserved; it does not give the direction of change. Heat flowing from cold to hot would conserve energy but never occurs unaided, so the second law is needed — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A process that proceeds on its own, without continuous outside help, under the given conditions is called a:

options.text_md: reversible process
spontaneous process
adiabatic process
cyclic process

questions.solution_md: A spontaneous (natural) process occurs by itself under the given conditions, in a definite direction. Reversible, adiabatic and cyclic describe the way a change is carried out, not whether it occurs unaided — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student notes that ice melts at room temperature although melting is endothermic, and that ammonium nitrate dissolves in water although the dissolution is also endothermic. The justified conclusion is that:

options.text_md: all endothermic processes are spontaneous at room temperature
ΔH has no relation at all to spontaneity
a negative ΔH alone cannot be the criterion of spontaneity; the increase of entropy also drives such changes
endothermic processes break the first law of thermodynamics

questions.solution_md: Both changes absorb heat yet occur spontaneously, so ΔH < 0 is not necessary for spontaneity. In each case the disorder of the system increases (solid → liquid, ordered crystal → free ions), and this entropy gain outweighs the energy cost — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following changes will not occur unaided at room temperature?

options.text_md: the scent molecules spread evenly through a classroom collecting again in one corner
an iron nail rusting in moist air
sugar dissolving in a cup of tea
a hot cup of tea cooling to room temperature

questions.solution_md: Rusting, dissolving and cooling are all natural, spontaneous changes. The spread of molecules through a room is irreversible: their collection into one corner by themselves would need outside work — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which statement is a form of the second law of thermodynamics?

options.text_md: heat cannot by itself flow from a colder body to a hotter body
energy can neither be created nor destroyed
the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at absolute zero
the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same by every route

questions.solution_md: The Clausius statement of the second law says that heat cannot flow of its own accord from a colder to a hotter body. The other options are the first law, the third law and Hess’s law — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a thermodynamically reversible process:

options.text_md: the change takes place at a finite rate in a single step
the surroundings do no work on the system
the system is at every stage in equilibrium with its surroundings, the changes being infinitesimally small
the process can be carried out only once

questions.solution_md: A reversible process is carried out through a series of infinitesimal steps, with the system always in equilibrium with its surroundings, so that the process can be reversed at any stage by an infinitesimal change in a condition — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A gas confined to one of two connected bulbs spreads into the evacuated bulb when the tap between them is opened.

**Reason (R):** The spreading of the gas increases the disorder, and hence the entropy, of the system.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. There is no energy change for an ideal gas, so the driving force is the increase in entropy: the gas has more ways of being arranged in the larger volume, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ice melts spontaneously above 273 K even though melting is endothermic.

**Reason (R):** The entropy of water decreases when ice melts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the molecules of liquid water are less ordered than those in the ice lattice, so the entropy increases on melting, and above 273 K the gain outweighs the heat absorbed — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A process that is spontaneous in one direction is also spontaneous in the reverse direction under the same conditions, provided enough time is allowed.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. A spontaneous change has a definite direction; the reverse change does not occur unaided under the same conditions and needs outside work.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons, with an example each, why the first law of thermodynamics alone cannot decide whether a chemical or physical change will take place.

answer.model_answer_md: First, the first law only requires energy to be conserved, and says nothing about direction: heat flowing from a cold body to a hot body would conserve energy, yet never occurs by itself. Second, a negative ΔH is not a sufficient guide: ice melts above 273 K and ammonium nitrate dissolves in water although both changes absorb heat, so the first law cannot predict them.

questions.solution_md: No direction of change; ΔH < 0 is neither necessary nor sufficient.

marking_scheme.step: No direction: heat from cold to hot conserves energy but does not occur
ΔH alone fails: endothermic changes such as melting of ice are spontaneous

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a spontaneous process from a non-spontaneous process, giving two examples of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A spontaneous process takes place of its own accord under the given conditions, in a definite direction (for example heat flowing from a hot to a cold body, or a gas expanding into a vacuum). A non-spontaneous process does not occur unaided and needs outside work or energy (for example a gas compressing itself into one corner of a vessel, or water flowing uphill).

questions.solution_md: Spontaneous: occurs unaided (two examples); non-spontaneous: needs outside work (two examples).

questions.stem_md: The entropy change of a system depends only on its initial and final states and not on the path followed between them. This shows that entropy is a:

options.text_md: path function
form of heat
state function
form of work

questions.solution_md: A property whose change depends only on the initial and final states is a state function, like U, H and G — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student classifies four changes. Which one shows a decrease in the entropy of the system?

options.text_md: sublimation of a pellet of solid carbon dioxide
dissolving a crystal of sugar in water
boiling water in a kettle

questions.solution_md: Two moles of gas combine to form one mole of gas, so the system becomes more ordered and ΔS < 0. Sublimation, dissolution and boiling all create more freedom of motion (ΔS > 0) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Solid benzene melts at 278.7 K, and the enthalpy of fusion is 9.87 kJ mol⁻¹. The entropy of fusion is about:

options.text_md: 0.035 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
354 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
9.87 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
35.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

questions.solution_md: At the melting point the change is reversible, so ΔS = q_rev / T = ΔfusH / T = 9870 J mol⁻¹ / 278.7 K = 35.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Melting one mole of ice gives the system an entropy gain of +22.0 J K⁻¹ and takes 6010 J of heat from the surroundings. In surroundings held at 263 K, the total entropy change of the universe for this melting is:

options.text_md: +0.85 J K⁻¹, so the ice melts spontaneously
+22.0 J K⁻¹, since the surroundings do not matter
zero, so ice and water are in equilibrium at 263 K
−0.85 J K⁻¹, so the ice does not melt spontaneously

questions.solution_md: ΔS(surroundings) = −q / T = −6010 / 263 = −22.85 J K⁻¹. ΔS(total) = +22.0 + (−22.85) = −0.85 J K⁻¹ < 0, so melting does not occur spontaneously at 263 K — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a demonstration, 0.50 mol of an ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly at 300 K until its volume doubles. The entropy change of the gas is:
questions.solution_md: For a reversible isothermal expansion q_rev = nRT ln(V₂/V₁), so ΔS = q_rev/T = nR ln(V₂/V₁) = 0.50 × 8.314 × ln 2 = 2.88 J K⁻¹ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The "thermal death" of the universe is the predicted final state in which:

options.text_md: the entropy of the universe has fallen to zero
all the energy of the universe has been destroyed
the entropy of the universe has reached its maximum and temperature is uniform, so no work can be obtained from heat
every reaction has been converted completely into its products

questions.solution_md: Since the entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous change, it tends to a maximum. At that stage temperature is the same everywhere, no heat flows, and no heat engine can work — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The standard molar entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) at 298 K are diamond 2.4, graphite 5.7, liquid water 69.9 and steam 188.8. The order of increasing entropy is:

options.text_md: steam < liquid water < graphite < diamond
graphite < diamond < steam < liquid water
liquid water < steam < diamond < graphite
diamond < graphite < liquid water < steam

questions.solution_md: Entropy rises with the freedom of motion of the particles: a rigid, compact crystal (diamond) is the most ordered, then graphite, then the liquid, with the gas the most disordered — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Propanone (acetone) boils at 329.4 K under 1 atm and its enthalpy of vaporisation is 29.1 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the entropy of vaporisation, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: At the boiling point the change is reversible: $\Delta S = \dfrac{q_{rev}}{T} = \dfrac{29\,100\ \text{J mol}^{-1}}{329.4\ \text{K}} = 88.3$ J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: ΔS = ΔvapH / T with ΔH in J

questions.stem_md: Mercury freezes at 234.3 K and the enthalpy of fusion is 2.29 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the entropy of fusion in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $\Delta S = \dfrac{\Delta_{fus}H}{T} = \dfrac{2290}{234.3} = 9.77$ J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: A chemist lets 3.0 mol of an ideal gas expand isothermally and reversibly at 350 K from 5.0 L to 25.0 L. Calculate the entropy change of the gas in J K⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
questions.solution_md: $\Delta S = nR\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = 3.0 \times 8.314 \times \ln 5 = 3.0 \times 8.314 \times 1.609 \approx 40.1$ J K⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of molar entropy is ___.
questions.solution_md: Entropy change = heat / temperature, so the unit of entropy is J K⁻¹ and of molar entropy J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The entropy change of a system is equal to the heat actually absorbed, divided by the temperature, for any process, reversible or irreversible.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. ΔS = q_rev / T: the heat must be the heat absorbed in a reversible path between the same states; for an irreversible change q/T is smaller than ΔS.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The entropy of vaporisation of water at 373 K is about 109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

**Reason (R):** Water vapour in the atmosphere is a greenhouse gas that absorbs infrared radiation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. The value follows from ΔvapS = ΔvapH / T = 40 700 / 373.15 ≈ 109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; the greenhouse behaviour of water vapour has nothing to do with it — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Define entropy and give its SI unit. Predict, with a reason, the sign of ΔS when a crystal of sodium chloride dissolves in water.

answer.model_answer_md: Entropy is a thermodynamic state function that measures the disorder (randomness) of a system; for a reversible change ΔS = q_rev / T, with the unit J K⁻¹. When NaCl dissolves, the ordered crystal lattice breaks up into freely moving hydrated ions, so the disorder increases and ΔS is positive.

questions.solution_md: Measure of disorder, J K⁻¹; ΔS positive (ordered lattice → free ions).

questions.stem_md: Predict the sign of ΔS for (a) the freezing of water, $\ce{H2O(l) -> H2O(s)}$, and (b) the decomposition $\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$, giving a reason in each case.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) ΔS is negative: the molecules go from the free motion of the liquid into a fixed, ordered lattice in ice, so the disorder falls. (b) ΔS is positive: a gas is produced from solids, and the gas has far more freedom of motion.

questions.solution_md: (a) negative (more order); (b) positive (gas formed).

questions.stem_md: A chemist melts 36 g of ice (M = 18 g mol⁻¹) at 273.15 K. The enthalpy of fusion of ice is 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the entropy change of the water.

answer.model_answer_md: Moles of ice = 36 / 18 = 2. Heat absorbed reversibly = 2 × 6010 = 12 020 J. ΔS = q_rev / T = 12 020 / 273.15 = 44.0 J K⁻¹ (that is, 22.0 J K⁻¹ for each mole).

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the "thermal death" of the universe, and on what law is the prediction based?

answer.model_answer_md: Thermal death is the predicted end state in which the entropy of the universe has reached its maximum value: temperature is uniform everywhere, no heat can flow, and no work can be got from heat, so all natural change stops. It is based on the second law, which says that the entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous process.

questions.solution_md: Maximum entropy, uniform temperature, no work obtainable; second law.

marking_scheme.step: Maximum entropy, uniform temperature, no further change
Based on the second law: entropy of the universe increases

questions.stem_md: One mole of ice at 273 K melts in a room at 283 K. The entropy change of the water (the system) is +22.0 J K⁻¹ and the heat taken from the room is 6010 J. Calculate the entropy change of the surroundings and of the universe, and state whether melting is spontaneous.

answer.model_answer_md: ΔS(surroundings) = −q / T = −6010 / 283 = −21.24 J K⁻¹. ΔS(universe) = ΔS(system) + ΔS(surroundings) = +22.0 + (−21.24) = +0.76 J K⁻¹. It is positive, so melting is spontaneous at 283 K.

questions.solution_md: ΔS(surroundings) = −21.24 J K⁻¹; ΔS(universe) = +0.76 J K⁻¹; spontaneous.

questions.stem_md: Use the standard entropies S° (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): N₂ 191.6, H₂ 130.7, NH₃ 192.5 to calculate ΔS° for $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)}$, and explain the sign of the answer.

answer.model_answer_md: ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants) = 2(192.5) − [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = 385.0 − 583.7 = -198.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. It is negative because four moles of gas change to two moles of gas, so there is less disorder in the product.

questions.solution_md: ΔS° = -198.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; negative as the number of gas moles falls.

marking_scheme.step: Fall in moles of gas, so less disorder

questions.stem_md: The standard molar entropies of liquid water and steam at 298 K are 69.9 and 188.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔS° for H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) at 298 K, and explain why the entropy of a gas is so much greater than that of the same substance as a liquid.

answer.model_answer_md: ΔS° = 188.8 − 69.9 = 118.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. In the liquid the molecules are close together with limited freedom of motion; in the gas they are far apart and move freely through a very much larger volume, so the number of possible arrangements, and hence the disorder, is far greater.

questions.solution_md: ΔS° = 118.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Greater freedom of motion and more arrangements in the gas

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain, with an example, why the first law of thermodynamics is inadequate to predict the direction of a change. [2]

(b) When 2000 J of heat flows from a hot body at 400 K to a cold body at 300 K, calculate the entropy change of each body and of the two together (the bodies are large enough for the temperatures to stay constant), and say what the sign of the total shows. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The first law only demands that energy is conserved. Heat flowing from a cold body to a hot body would conserve energy just as well as the reverse, yet only the hot-to-cold direction is observed; similarly ice melts above 273 K although it absorbs heat. The first law gives no direction, so a second criterion (entropy) is needed.

(b) ΔS(hot) = −2000 / 400 = -5.00 J K⁻¹; ΔS(cold) = +2000 / 300 = +6.67 J K⁻¹. ΔS(total) = -5.00 + 6.67 = +1.67 J K⁻¹. The total is positive, so the heat flow is spontaneous, as observed.

questions.solution_md: ΔS(hot) = -5.00; ΔS(cold) = +6.67; total = +1.67 J K⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Example (heat flow or melting of ice)
(b) ΔS(cold) = +6.67 J K⁻¹ and total +1.67 J K⁻¹

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define entropy, and state why it is called a state function. [2]

(b) Calculate the entropy of fusion of ice (ΔfusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273.15 K) and the entropy of vaporisation of water (ΔvapH = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 373.15 K), and explain why the second is so much larger. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Entropy is a measure of the disorder of a system; for a reversible process ΔS = q_rev / T. It is a state function because its change depends only on the initial and final states of the system, not on the path.

(b) ΔS(fusion) = 6010 / 273.15 = 22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔS(vaporisation) = 40 700 / 373.15 = 109.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. On melting, the molecules remain close together and gain only some freedom; on vaporisation they become completely free and spread through a much larger volume, so the increase in disorder is about five times greater.

questions.solution_md: ΔS(fusion) = 22.0; ΔS(vaporisation) = 109.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: (a) State function: depends on initial and final states only
(b) Gas has far more freedom than liquid

questions.stem_md: At constant temperature and pressure, a process is spontaneous when:

options.text_md: ΔG is positive
ΔG is negative
ΔH is negative, whatever the value of ΔS
ΔS of the system alone is positive, whatever the value of ΔH

questions.solution_md: The Gibbs energy criterion is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 at constant T and p. Neither the sign of ΔH alone nor that of ΔS(system) alone decides the direction — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen peroxide solution in a pharmacy bottle decomposes slowly: 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), with ΔH = −196 kJ and ΔS = +126 J K⁻¹ (both illustrative). Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the decomposition is spontaneous:

options.text_md: only at high temperatures
only at low temperatures
at no temperature
at all temperatures, since ΔH is negative and ΔS positive

questions.solution_md: With ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, the term −TΔS is also negative, so ΔG = −196 − T(0.126) is negative at every temperature. (Spontaneous does not mean fast: the bottle keeps because the rate is slow) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$, ΔH = -114.2 kJ and ΔS = -146.5 J K⁻¹ (taken as constant). The reaction is spontaneous only:

options.text_md: above about 780 K
below about -1.28 K
below about 780 K
at all temperatures

questions.solution_md: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS = (−114 200 J)/(−146.5 J K⁻¹) = 780 K. Both ΔH and ΔS are negative, so −TΔS is positive and grows with T: ΔG is negative only below this temperature — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{N2O4(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ at 300 K, ΔG = +4.8 kJ (given). Using G = A + pV, so that ΔG = ΔA + Δn_g RT for ideal gases, ΔA is:
The Helmholtz energy is defined as A = U − TS. At constant temperature and constant volume a process is spontaneous when:

options.text_md: ΔA is positive
ΔA is zero
ΔU is positive
ΔA is negative

questions.solution_md: At constant T and V the criterion of spontaneity is ΔA < 0 (the analogue of ΔG < 0 at constant T and p); ΔA = 0 at equilibrium — option (d).

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$ at 298 K, ΔH° = -571.6 kJ and ΔS° = -326.7 J K⁻¹. The value of ΔG° is:
questions.solution_md: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −571.6 − 298 × (−326.7 / 1000) = −571.6 + 97.4 = −474.2 kJ. The ΔS term must be converted to kJ (÷ 1000) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: At constant temperature and pressure, the decrease in the Gibbs energy, −ΔG, of a system measures:

options.text_md: the heat absorbed by the system
the maximum useful (non-expansion) work that can be obtained from the process
the work of expansion done against the atmosphere
the entropy change of the surroundings only

questions.solution_md: G = H − TS; at constant T and p, −ΔG equals the maximum net work obtainable other than pV work (for example electrical work from a cell) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{N2O4(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ at 298 K, ΔH° = +57.2 kJ and ΔS° = +175.9 J K⁻¹ (from tables). Calculate ΔG° in kJ, and decide whether the dissociation is spontaneous at 298 K.
questions.solution_md: $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = 57.2 - 298 \times 0.1759 = 57.2 - 52.42 = 4.78$ kJ. Positive, so not spontaneous at 298 K.

marking_scheme.step: TΔS = 52.42 kJ with ΔS in kJ

questions.stem_md: Magnesium carbonate decomposes: $\ce{MgCO3(s) -> MgO(s) + CO2(g)}$, with ΔH = +100.7 kJ and ΔS = +175.0 J K⁻¹ (both from tables, taken as independent of temperature). Calculate the temperature, in K, above which the decomposition becomes spontaneous.
questions.solution_md: At the crossover $\Delta G = 0$, so $T = \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S} = \dfrac{100\,700}{175.0} = 575.4 \approx 575$ K.

marking_scheme.step: ΔG = 0, T = ΔH/ΔS with ΔH in J

questions.stem_md: The thermodynamic function G = H − TS is called the ___ free energy.
questions.solution_md: G = H − TS is the Gibbs free energy (or Gibbs energy); the criterion of spontaneity at constant T and p is ΔG < 0.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At constant temperature and pressure, a process is spontaneous if ΔG is negative.

**Reason (R):** ΔG = −TΔS(total), where ΔS(total) is the entropy change of the system and surroundings together.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. ΔS(surroundings) = −ΔH/T, so TΔS(total) = TΔS − ΔH = −ΔG; ΔG < 0 therefore means ΔS(total) > 0, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match the signs of ΔH and ΔS of a reaction with its spontaneity according to ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

options.text_md: ΔH negative, ΔS positive
ΔH positive, ΔS negative
ΔH negative, ΔS negative
ΔH positive, ΔS positive

questions.solution_md: (−, +): ΔG always negative → s; (+, −): ΔG always positive → p; (−, −): spontaneous below ΔH/ΔS → r; (+, +): spontaneous above ΔH/ΔS → q.

questions.stem_md: Match each thermodynamic quantity with its defining expression.

options.text_md: Gibbs energy, G
Helmholtz energy, A
Entropy change of a reversible change, ΔS
G in terms of A

questions.solution_md: G = H − TS (q); A = U − TS (s); ΔS = q_rev/T (p); G = A + pV (r).

questions.stem_md: Write the expression that defines the Helmholtz free energy A, and state the criterion of spontaneity in terms of ΔA at constant temperature and volume.

answer.model_answer_md: A = U − TS, where U is the internal energy, T the temperature and S the entropy. At constant temperature and volume a process is spontaneous if ΔA < 0 (and at equilibrium ΔA = 0); −ΔA is the maximum work obtainable from the system at constant temperature.

questions.solution_md: A = U − TS; spontaneous if ΔA < 0 at constant T and V.

marking_scheme.step: ΔA < 0 for spontaneity at constant T and V

questions.stem_md: Starting from G = H − TS and H = U + pV, show that the Gibbs energy G and the Helmholtz energy A are related by G = A + pV.

answer.model_answer_md: G = H − TS = (U + pV) − TS = (U − TS) + pV. Since A = U − TS, G = A + pV. For a change at constant temperature, ΔG = ΔA + Δ(pV).

questions.solution_md: G = U + pV − TS = A + pV.

marking_scheme.step: Substitute H = U + pV in G = H − TS
Group U − TS = A, giving G = A + pV

questions.stem_md: Using ΔfH° (N₂O₄ +9.2, NO₂ +33.2 kJ mol⁻¹) and S° (N₂O₄ 304.3, NO₂ 240.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), calculate ΔH° and ΔS° for $\ce{N2O4(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$, and the temperature above which the dissociation is spontaneous.

answer.model_answer_md: ΔH° = 2(33.2) − 9.2 = +57.2 kJ. ΔS° = 2(240.1) − 304.3 = +175.9 J K⁻¹. At the crossover ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = 57 200 / 175.9 = 325 K. Both ΔH and ΔS are positive, so the dissociation is spontaneous above about 325 K.

marking_scheme.step: Spontaneous above this temperature (ΔH, ΔS positive)

questions.stem_md: The decomposition 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) has ΔH = −196.0 kJ and ΔS = +125.8 J K⁻¹ (both illustrative). Explain why ΔS is positive, calculate ΔG at 298 K, and say whether the reaction can be made non-spontaneous by changing the temperature.

answer.model_answer_md: ΔS is positive because a gas is formed from liquids, so the disorder increases. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −196.0 − 298 × 0.1258 = −196.0 − 37.5 = -233.5 kJ. Since ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG is negative at every temperature, so no change of temperature makes the decomposition non-spontaneous (it may still be slow).

questions.solution_md: ΔG = -233.5 kJ at 298 K; negative at all temperatures.

marking_scheme.step: Negative at all T since ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{N2O4(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ at 298 K, find ΔG° in two ways: (i) from ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° with ΔH° = +57.2 kJ and ΔS° = +175.9 J K⁻¹; (ii) from ΔfG° (N₂O₄ +97.9, NO₂ +51.3 kJ mol⁻¹). Comment on the result.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) ΔG° = 57.2 − 298 × 0.1759 = 57.2 − 52.42 = +4.78 kJ. (ii) ΔG° = 2(51.3) − 97.9 = +4.7 kJ. The two agree within rounding (about +4.7 to +4.8 kJ); the positive value shows that the dissociation is not spontaneous at 298 K, so N₂O₄ is the favoured form at room temperature.

questions.solution_md: (i) +4.78 kJ; (ii) +4.7 kJ; non-spontaneous at 298 K.

marking_scheme.step: Agreement; positive so non-spontaneous at 298 K

questions.stem_md: The formation of liquid water, $\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$, has ΔH° = −571.6 kJ and ΔS° = −326.7 J K⁻¹ at 298 K. Although ΔS° is negative, the reaction is spontaneous once started. Calculate ΔG° and explain the paradox.

answer.model_answer_md: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −571.6 − 298 × (−0.3267) = −571.6 + 97.4 = -474.2 kJ. The negative ΔS° (three moles of gas become liquid) makes the −TΔS° term positive (+97.4 kJ), but it is far smaller than the large negative ΔH°, so ΔG° is strongly negative and the reaction is spontaneous.

questions.solution_md: ΔG° = -474.2 kJ; the large negative ΔH° outweighs −TΔS°.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define the Gibbs free energy G and the Helmholtz free energy A, and show that G = A + pV. [3]

(b) For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g) at 300 K, ΔG = −70.0 kJ (given). Calculate ΔA, treating the gases as ideal (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) G = H − TS and A = U − TS. Since H = U + pV, G = U + pV − TS = (U − TS) + pV = A + pV.

(b) Δn_g = 2 − 3 = −1, so Δ(pV) = Δn_g RT = −1 × 8.314 × 300 = -2494 J = -2.49 kJ. ΔA = ΔG − Δ(pV) = −70.0 − (-2.49) = -67.5 kJ.

questions.solution_md: G = A + pV; ΔA = -67.5 kJ.

questions.stem_md:
Magnesium carbonate decomposes on heating: $\ce{MgCO3(s) -> MgO(s) + CO2(g)}$.

(a) Calculate ΔH° and ΔS° from ΔfH° (MgCO₃ −1095.8, MgO −601.6, CO₂ −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹) and S° (MgCO₃ 65.7, MgO 26.9, CO₂ 213.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). [3]

(b) Calculate ΔG° at 298 K and the temperature above which the decomposition is spontaneous. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) ΔH° = (−601.6 − 393.5) − (−1095.8) = +100.7 kJ. ΔS° = (26.9 + 213.8) − 65.7 = +175.0 J K⁻¹.

(b) ΔG° = 100.7 − 298 × 0.1750 = 100.7 − 52.15 = +48.6 kJ, positive, so MgCO₃ is stable at 298 K. At the crossover ΔG = 0: T = 100 700 / 175.0 = 575 K, so the decomposition is spontaneous above about 575 K.

questions.stem_md: For a reaction at 298 K, the standard Gibbs energy change ΔG° is negative. The equilibrium constant of the reaction is therefore:

options.text_md: less than 1
greater than 1
equal to 1
equal to zero

questions.solution_md: ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K. A negative ΔG° makes log K positive, so K > 1 and the products are favoured at equilibrium — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A reaction has ΔG° = +22.8 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Using ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), the equilibrium constant is about:
Which statement is the third law of thermodynamics?

options.text_md: the entropy of every substance is zero at 273 K
the entropy of the universe remains constant
the entropy of a gas is zero at 0 °C and 1 atm
the entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is zero at the absolute zero of temperature

questions.solution_md: The third law states that the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at 0 K, which allows absolute entropies to be tabulated — option (d).

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{N2O4(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$, ΔH° = +57.2 kJ and ΔS° = +175.9 J K⁻¹ (taken as constant). The equilibrium constant at 350 K is about:
The standard Gibbs energy change of a reaction at 298 K is −28.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (given). Calculate log K for the reaction (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
According to the third law, the entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is zero at ___ K.
questions.solution_md: The third law states that the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at the absolute zero, 0 K.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The entropy of a perfect crystal of a pure substance is zero at 0 K, and it increases as the temperature is raised.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. This is the third law; as the temperature rises the particles gain motion and the entropy increases, with further jumps at melting and boiling.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at room temperature.

**Reason (R):** The entropy of a pure substance decreases as its temperature is raised.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is false: the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero only at 0 K. R is false: entropy increases with temperature as the thermal motion grows — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The equilibrium constant of a reaction with ΔG° = 0 is equal to 1.

**Reason (R):** At equilibrium the standard Gibbs energy change ΔG° of every reaction is zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: ΔG° = 0 gives log K = 0, so K = 1. R is false: at equilibrium it is ΔG (not ΔG°) that is zero; ΔG° is zero only when K = 1 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: State the third law of thermodynamics and say what it allows chemists to tabulate.

answer.model_answer_md: The third law states that the entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is zero at the absolute zero of temperature. It provides a reference point, so the absolute (standard molar) entropies of substances at other temperatures can be calculated and tabulated.

questions.solution_md: S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K; absolute entropies can be tabulated.

questions.stem_md: The acid dissociation constant of ethanoic acid is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 298 K. Calculate ΔG° for its ionisation in water (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) and say what the sign tells you.

answer.model_answer_md: ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K = −2.303 × 8.314 × 298 × log(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = −5706 × (−4.745) = +27073 J mol⁻¹ ≈ +27.1 kJ mol⁻¹. The positive sign means that the ionisation is not spontaneous from the standard state (K < 1): at equilibrium the acid is mostly un-ionised.

questions.solution_md: ΔG° = +27.1 kJ mol⁻¹; K < 1.

marking_scheme.step: 2.303 RT = 5706 J mol⁻¹ and log K = −4.745

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{N2O4(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ at 298 K, ΔG° = +4.78 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the equilibrium constant K (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) and state which species predominates at equilibrium.

answer.model_answer_md: log K = −ΔG° / (2.303 RT) = −4780 / 5706 = -0.838, so K = 0.15. Since K < 1, the equilibrium mixture contains mainly N₂O₄ (the reactant).

questions.solution_md: log K = -0.838; K = 0.15; N₂O₄ predominates.

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{N2O4(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$, ΔH° = +57.2 kJ and ΔS° = +175.9 J K⁻¹ (assumed constant). Calculate ΔG° and K at 350 K, and say how the position of equilibrium differs from that at 298 K (K = 0.15).

answer.model_answer_md: ΔG° = 57.2 − 350 × 0.1759 = -4.36 kJ. log K = 4.36 / (2.303 × 8.314 × 350 / 1000) = 0.651, so K = 4.5. At 350 K, ΔG° is negative and K > 1, so NO₂ predominates; at 298 K, K < 1 and N₂O₄ predominates. The endothermic dissociation is favoured at the higher temperature.

questions.solution_md: ΔG° = -4.36 kJ; K = 4.5; NO₂ favoured at 350 K.

marking_scheme.step: Comparison: NO₂ favoured at the higher temperature

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the relation between the standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant, and state what a negative and a positive ΔG° imply for K. [2]

(b) A reaction in a laboratory has ΔG° = −17.1 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K (given). Calculate its equilibrium constant (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) ΔG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K. If ΔG° < 0, log K > 0 and K > 1 (products favoured); if ΔG° > 0, K < 1 (reactants favoured); if ΔG° = 0, K = 1.

(b) log K = 17 100 / (2.303 × 8.314 × 298) = 17 100 / 5706 = 3.00, so K = 10^3.00 ≈ 993 ≈ 1.0 × 10³.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Meaning of negative and positive ΔG°

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the third law of thermodynamics. [1]

(b) Using S° (liquid water 69.9, steam 188.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), calculate ΔS° for H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) at 298 K. [2]

(c) Explain why the third law lets us tabulate absolute entropies, although absolute enthalpies cannot be tabulated. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is zero at the absolute zero of temperature.

(b) ΔS° = 188.8 − 69.9 = 118.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (positive: gas formed from liquid).

(c) The third law fixes a natural zero of entropy (S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K), so S at any temperature can be found by adding up q_rev/T from 0 K. For enthalpy and internal energy there is no such natural zero, so only changes (ΔH) can be measured and tabulated.

questions.solution_md: (b) ΔS° = 118.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Natural zero of entropy at 0 K
(c) No such zero for H or U, so only ΔH can be measured
